title: Types of Sentences
description: Identify simple, compound, and complex sentences by analyzing their clauses.
directions: For each question, choose whether the sentence is simple, compound, or complex.
submissionInstruction: Save this result as a PDF and submit it as directed by your teacher.

questions.prompt: The students packed their notebooks and hurried to the buses.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains one independent clause. “The students” is the subject, and “packed” and “hurried” form a compound predicate.

questions.prompt: The rain stopped, and the players returned to the field.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains two independent clauses: “The rain stopped” and “the players returned to the field.” They are joined by the coordinating conjunction “and.”

questions.prompt: Although the rain had stopped, the field remained muddy.
questions.explanation: “Although the rain had stopped” is a dependent clause, and “the field remained muddy” is an independent clause.

questions.prompt: My brother and I baked cookies after dinner.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains one independent clause. “My brother and I” is a compound subject, but the sentence still has only one complete clause.

questions.prompt: The librarian closed the windows, but she left the front door open.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains two independent clauses: “The librarian closed the windows” and “she left the front door open.” They are joined by “but.”

questions.prompt: When the final bell rang, the hallway filled with students.
questions.explanation: “When the final bell rang” is a dependent clause, and “the hallway filled with students” is an independent clause.

questions.prompt: The old dog slept beside the fireplace all afternoon.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains one subject, “dog,” and one verb, “slept.” It has one independent clause.

questions.prompt: Maya wanted to finish the book; she stayed up past midnight.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains two independent clauses joined by a semicolon: “Maya wanted to finish the book” and “she stayed up past midnight.”

questions.prompt: Because the roads were icy, school opened two hours late.
questions.explanation: “Because the roads were icy” is a dependent clause, and “school opened two hours late” is an independent clause.

questions.prompt: The bright signs and loud music attracted a crowd.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains one independent clause. “The bright signs and loud music” is a compound subject, not two separate clauses.

questions.prompt: We could walk to the theater, or we could take the bus.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains two independent clauses: “We could walk to the theater” and “we could take the bus.” They are joined by “or.”

questions.prompt: The class grew quiet as the principal entered the room.
questions.explanation: “The class grew quiet” is an independent clause, and “as the principal entered the room” is a dependent clause.

questions.prompt: The chef chopped the vegetables, stirred the soup, and checked the oven.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains one independent clause. The subject “chef” performs three actions, creating a compound predicate.

questions.prompt: The power went out, so everyone used flashlights.
questions.explanation: This sentence contains two independent clauses: “The power went out” and “everyone used flashlights.” They are joined by “so.”

questions.prompt: I will call you after I finish my homework.
questions.explanation: “I will call you” is an independent clause, and “after I finish my homework” is a dependent clause.
